image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal percentile range / interval bar chart** (one horizontal bar per major, showing earnings distribution from the 10th to 90th percentile, with internal percentile breakpoints).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** with **horizontal small-multiple-like rows** for each college major.
- No faceting.
- Not stacked by category in the usual additive sense; instead, each row is a **segmented interval bar** split at percentile boundaries (10th, 25th, median, 75th, 90th).

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| College major / field of study (e.g., Education, Economics, Chemical Engineering) | Categorical / nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels for rows |
| Projected career earnings | Quantitative | Position on x-axis; horizontal length/extent of bars |
| Percentile level (10th, 25th, Median, 75th, 90th) | Ordinal | Segment boundaries within each horizontal bar; top annotations/labels |
| Earnings range between percentiles | Quantitative | Width of each bar segment between percentile cut points |
| Segment category by percentile band | Ordinal | Color/lightness differences across bar segments |

comments.raw_comment: The graph objectively depicts the approximate lifetime earnings of various vocations within different fields of study. A median, as well as a 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentile, are plotted on the graph as they locate and quantize the range of projected salaries that populations within each field receive. The varying majors located on the left display a common trend, in that the majors related to science and economy gravitate towards the higher end of the spectrum while other jobs, namely government paid vocations, lean towards the lower end. There remains an outlier on the last major, chemical engineering, as their median as well as their range are noticeably higher than all other majors. As the title states how these earnings are for college graduates, it can be inferred that the graph is intended for students looking for different types of jobs and depicts the monetary incentive for each career type. Nonetheless, a large amount of factors are omitted within this graph as certain components, such as what amount of time constitutes a career, are never specified. This fallacy impedes the overall credibility of the graph and detracts from the data presented to the reader.

comments.raw_comment: Based off the graph, the same amount of college education can result in differences of salaries across majors. The median numbers increases as the list goes down and they usually lean towards the left of the blue. The higher earning figures tend to be in the S.T.E.M. field as compared to the others. Due to the growing demand of progress, those careers are often paid larger amounts for their work. The top earning S.T.E.M. majors seem to have more competition compared to wider fields such as philosophy and are harder to get a job in than the rest. Even though those fields are going to be useful in the future, we as a society need to appreciate other fields like Education and Social more. Those fields are just as important in lending a hand in progressing our society and they deserve a higher salary than they are getting currently. The graph does not tell the whole story, factors such as location, economy, if its a government or company job, and degree of difficulty effects how much a person makes during a career. The graph is likely to change in the future because of the changing economy we have today. If a majority in College chose Chemical Engineering due to this graph, the career earnings would go down drastically due to a drop in competition. I would not recommend this graph for choosing a career because of the factors that do not go into it.

Therefore, we can imply that government salaries tend to be lower than science majors such as chemical engineering or computer science, which are located near the lower part of the graph with higher median ranges. Because the graph shows different career paths, their main audience are incoming teens who have to decide their majors for college. In the end, based on this graph students may choose one of these careers solely on money.  However, I wonder if this information is completely accurate for students in fours years who may have to decide their fields of study now. Not only that but there are many other factors that contribute to deciding one's field of study. Therefore, I don't think this graph is beneficial as one piece of evidence for jobs or career paths solely based on over generalized wages which in the end may end up changing overtime.

comments.raw_comment: Douglas Webber in his “The Lifetime Earnings Premia of Different Majors” analyzes projected career income from solely an economical standpoint. Looking at the graph, I noticed that the bottom half of the careers focus mostly on the STEM subjects. The careers that earn a lesser amount money appear to be geared more towards social-oriented subjects, such as philosophy and education. The white dashes on the bars are the median earnings, and the darker shades of blue are the points nearest to the median. It is questionable if this graph is really proportional, as well as if the graph is accurate. I am unaware of where the author received his information, causing me to feel quite skeptical of the graph. I am curious as to how many incomes were utilized in order to create this bar graph and if taxes were included or removed from the overall earnings. This graph could be indicating how as a society, we have drifted away from more social careers in favor of technology.

comments.raw_comment: The general trend of the graph seems to reflect that STEM-based career paths tend to result in higher projected career earnings than language-based or social science-based careers. This trend implies that people do not value the language and social-based careers enough even though I believe they do play a significant role in the infrastructure of society and the development of citizens’ minds. Also, while the median career earning does increase from the top to bottom of the graph, the range between the 10th and 90th percentiles also generally increases. The greater dispersion of career earnings may be a result of many people wanting to go into higher paying careers. Greater competition would be generated, causing a wider spectrum in the amount of money people in the same career path can earn. Thus, job availability should be taken into consideration along with the projected earnings. It is not wise to choose a career path based solely on the information shown by this graph because it is lacking the consideration of factors without a monetary incentive, such as satisfaction and passion—it is important for people to love their careers. I wonder how the data on this graph was collected and whether it only reflects the projected earnings for only a certain group of college graduates in society or whether it reflects all college graduates. I am curious to know if factors such as the university someone attends or their race/ethnicity can alter what the graph currently displays.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that as the careers become more related to fields in STEM, the median earnings increase. While I agree to some extent that the graph portrays a realistic visual of average career earnings, I believe that it has failed to take into account other factors beside the field of the career. Jobs like computer science and chemical engineer are becoming more popular amongst college students, which might make the supply for these jobs less demanding. With more people applying for similar positions, companies can pay workers lower salaries. Another factor, besides supply and demand, is passion. What the graph fails to consider is that some college students choose a certain career path out of passion or love for a subject. By categorizing the careers based on their earnings, Webber is associating careers with the amount of money that is earned. I agree that money should factor into considering a career, but it should not be the sole factor in determining a certain path.

comments.raw_comment: As indicated by the graph, the median wage for different careers fields increases as the graph progresses from top to bottom. In addition, most of the careers with median wages of $3 million or higher are STEM based, while careers with median wages that fall below $3M are based primarily on sociology, language, history, or the arts. I wonder if such discrepancy between career types is due to a higher demand for workers in scientific and mathematical fields, than others that fall outside of STEM. Although there are exceptions to this rule, the general pattern of the graph supports the idea that the economy favors STEM based careers. In my opinion, the graph seems to advise college students deciding on a major to enter these fields, using solely money as a motivation. I personally disagree with the notion that one should reconsider their major based on earnings alone because these statistics are subject to change and if one has no business in chemical engineering, then they should not enter such a career they are not adept at, nor take interest, in for the pay. I wonder how heavily the graph will impact the choices of students, and how it will change over time.

comments.raw_comment: As I was observing these graphs I noticed that between the 10th and 25th percentile, even a chemical engineer can make as much as the average person studying psychology. Even though Chemical Engineering can be considered as a much more difficult job than Psychology, it all depends on if the place where they live really needs a Psychologist or a Chemical Engineer. So for this reason, when looking at the 75th to 90th percentile I see that the Chemical Engineer can make 5 or 6 times more than a Psychologist not because it might be a more difficult job, but because there is a plethora of psychologists, and a scarce amount of Chemical Engineers. With the idea of supply and demand comes the fact that companies or businesses rely more on efficiency to meet the demand. This means that all workers have an expiration date and when they reach the peak of their productivity, they could easily be replaced by others willing to work harder and more efficiently.

comments.raw_comment: This graph argues for which careers college students should follow in order to earn the most money over their lifetime. Douglas Webber analyzes the benefits of different careers from an economic standpoint, demonstrating which career college graduates can ultimately gain the most wealth from. Webber contends that money should be the greatest influence in one’s career choice through his indirect support of students choosing careers which will give them the greatest wealth over factors such as passion or interest. His graph may also give inaccurate results as he is simply speculating over the amount of money people could make in their lifetime in a career, as demand could rise or fall, leading to an increase of decrease in income made. He also demonstrates a bias by his favoring of mainly STEM majors as careers with the highest earnings. Surely, there are many other careers which earn large sums of money and are not STEM, and by not including these majors, he attempts to persuade the observer to choose STEM careers in order earn the most wealth.

comments.raw_comment: The graph displayed depicts the career earnings for college graduates in specific areas of study. Firstly, the graph has two colors, light blue and dark blue, the dark blue representing the average earnings, and the light blue to represent the outliers, or the highest and lowest, in the pay scale. Another observation is that the careers that live in the areas of math and science tend to make more money over time than the careers based in the areas of literature, art, and critical thinking. This graph, while giving a good prediction of the earning, is flawed. It does not take into account the different factors that affect the earnings in some careers such as: level of education, working environment, passion for that field, inflation over time, the effect of government control over some careers like education, or criminal justice, and it does not take into account the different jobs that can be obtained with these different careers. While this graph gives a general overview of the earnings that can be obtained when following certain areas of study, it is not a good reference to choose a future career.

comments.raw_comment: The graph represents the projected career earnings for college graduates based on their major. Although, the graph appears to be a credible source, the sheer fact that the data is a “projection” implies that it could be incredibly inaccurate. The demand and funding for specific career options is constantly fluctuating and especially in the event of a severe economic crisis, specific earnings could plummet or skyrocket unexpectedly. Additionally, the graph can be misleading in the fact that the lowest and highest 10 percent of the projected career earnings are left off the chart. Therefore, if someone enters in the field expecting to make a certain amount, they may be unhappily surprised to realize they are in the lowest percentile and earning severely less than expected. Furthermore, low projections may discourage students from majoring in a field that may be best suited for them, and lose the opportunity to thrive at a job they excel at. I wonder what the reach of this graph is, and whether or not it will impact the decision of college students.

comments.raw_comment: As I read the graph, I notice the placement of the career paths as well as the differences in amounts each career earns. Different factors play into the wide range of earnings. Because most education and criminal justice majors tend to work for the government, earnings can be less compared to a computer science major who works for a company with a larger budget. The vast difference in earnings implies what careers are more popular in today’s society as well as possibly persuading future graduate students to pick their majors according to earnings. However, the credibility of the graph is questioned as “projected career earnings” can change in the future because of the unknown problems that can occur. Because of this, I wonder if future graduates do rely on such graphs when choosing the major they wish to study.

Students should not use the graph as their sole source of advice when it comes to career choice, especially since they will leave college jobless and in desperate need of a way to pay off their debt. However, the graph does aid in revealing the current state of careers since it is based on recently updated information. It also has a more expansive amount of data available to viewers to inform them of the current job climate. It does have its uses, but it should not be viewed as the law of the land.

comments.raw_comment: The overall career earnings projections in the chart reflect a deeply rooted mentality in today’s American society. We have the mentality of looking towards STEM majors to fix our issues at hand or to enhance our lives. For the most part, we are disregarding the types of jobs that will help us address issues in our society as a whole. For example, career choices of education, social work, or philosophy are projected to earn much less than careers such as chemical, or electrical engineering. This illustrates a very prevalent issue. We don’t want to be examined or have our communities changed but rather we support industries that serve to enhance our day to day lives. New technology products help individuals better their lives whereas careers that produce thought and incite understanding have much less appeal to our increasingly materialistic world. Non-STEM careers remain relatively unattractive to the current society because we don’t want to necessarily take the time or energy to think about our society.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that a majority of the careers that pay the most seem to be STEM careers possibly due to their significant importance in today's society. Businesses want to develop the latest and most advanced technology, and will most likely want to hire and pay a healthy salary to those they deem a reliable asset. This graph seems to emphasize the importance of a career in STEM and how it is a highly desired career in the business world for those who want to make a decent amount of money. Another key thing to notice is the fact that chemical engineering is the only career to have a median of $4 million while the next highest careers only have a median of $3.5 million. This shows that a career in STEM that is much harder to achieve pays the most, indicating the idea that if people want to earn the most money, then they must be willing to dedicate their time and effort into pursuing their goal.

comments.raw_comment:
One of my first observations was that the professions are ordered by median in increasing order. I also observe that there is considerable variation within each profession and think that perhaps there is less (though still significant) variation between the professions. As a college student studying math and humanities, I found it comforting to observe that there is a lot of overlap - it might be less likely, but a philosophy major sometimes earns more than an economics major. 

I notice that nursing is far down (higher lifetime earnings) and that surprises me. I'd like to know more about who was counted as a nursing major and whether those students trained solely to be nurses or whether perhaps some were pre-med and went on to be doctors.

That brings me to my biggest point: thinking in terms of majors can be deceptive. English majors can become chemistry PhDs. Psychology majors can join PR firms. I've read that kids from wealthier backgrounds often have more freedom to do "riskier" humanities majors - some of them then end up in law or finance. Overall, I think this graph might be trying to tell a story about how choice of major can affect lifetime earnings, but I think there is a lot not said that my fellow students should consider. We need to remember that major does not dictate career path, and thus the graph does not necessarily reflect how much people actually working in the areas they majored in earn.

comments.raw_comment: The New York Times graph projecting the career earnings of different college majors is very much targeted toward a high school audience. In other words, the teens of America who will soon make the jump to college and subsequently decide their career, finally having to answer the most annoying question they have been asked their entire lives: “What do you want to be when you grow up?” However, the graph is certainly not the end all be all. In fact, it should not even play the most significant role when deciding a college major. There are numerous other factors to consider that play a role. Of course there are a person’s interests, but there are also more concrete factors. For example, there is job growth. Chemical engineering, which according to the graph seems he most enticing, has a much slower growth than say computer science and thus is not nearly as secure. In addition, work hours st be considered. The biggest reason education earns the least is due to the fact that it is a government job. Yet, government jobs have far lower hours compared to private sector jobs and may thus be more enticing than it seems when glancing at this graph. America’s youth must realize that the nuances of careers are increasingly important as competition is rising in the new global economy. The future is daunting, but America’s youth can surely prepare.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all teachers and students who responded to our graph on the earning power of college graduates by major.  How much you make in a career isn’t the only criteria for selecting a major, but did this graph change your thinking about your college major and future career?

Lots of questions came up from this graph.  You asked how the majors were selected, how projected earnings were calculated, and how many years is considered a lifetime.  You wondered about what the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentile means and why the blue segments are of different lengths.  But, most frequently, you noticed that education majors made less than STEM majors.  As O'BryantGirlNamedFallon from Boston wrote, “Well, to me it seems like the teachers, who shape the future of our children, are not getting the money they deserve. I wonder, why should the teachers who help all these people reach their dreams, why should they get the lowest pay?” 

Since we continue to post responses, is there more that you notice?  More that you wonder?  Talk to your classmates and read the moderators’ responses. Maybe something they say will lead to more things you notice, wonder, and conjecture. 

Check back on Thursday, January 11 to learn more about this graph. We hope to see you again next month on Tuesday, February 13 for our next "What's Going On In This Graph?"   Signing off now -- Sharon in Boston and Erica in Pittsburgh. See you in February for our special Valentine’s Day graph!

comments.raw_comment: The graph objectively depicts the approximate lifetime earnings of various vocations within different fields of study. A median, as well as a 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentile, are plotted on the graph as they locate and quantize the range of projected salaries that populations within each field receive. The varying majors located on the left display a common trend, in that the majors related to science and economy gravitate towards the higher end of the spectrum while other jobs, namely government paid vocations, lean towards the lower end. There remains an outlier on the last major, chemical engineering, as their median as well as their range are noticeably higher than all other majors. As the title states how these earnings are for college graduates, it can be inferred that the graph is intended for students looking for different types of jobs and depicts the monetary incentive for each career type. Nonetheless, a large amount of factors are omitted within this graph as certain components, such as what amount of time constitutes a career, are never specified. This fallacy impedes the overall credibility of the graph and detracts from the data presented to the reader.

comments.raw_comment: Based off the graph, the same amount of college education can result in differences of salaries across majors. The median numbers increases as the list goes down and they usually lean towards the left of the blue. The higher earning figures tend to be in the S.T.E.M. field as compared to the others. Due to the growing demand of progress, those careers are often paid larger amounts for their work. The top earning S.T.E.M. majors seem to have more competition compared to wider fields such as philosophy and are harder to get a job in than the rest. Even though those fields are going to be useful in the future, we as a society need to appreciate other fields like Education and Social more. Those fields are just as important in lending a hand in progressing our society and they deserve a higher salary than they are getting currently. The graph does not tell the whole story, factors such as location, economy, if its a government or company job, and degree of difficulty effects how much a person makes during a career. The graph is likely to change in the future because of the changing economy we have today. If a majority in College chose Chemical Engineering due to this graph, the career earnings would go down drastically due to a drop in competition. I would not recommend this graph for choosing a career because of the factors that do not go into it.

comments.raw_comment: Some things I notice are from the top to the bottom of the graph the median wages increase. Therefore, we can imply that government salaries tend to be lower than science majors such as chemical engineering or computer science, which are located near the lower part of the graph with higher median ranges. Because the graph shows different career paths, their main audience are incoming teens who have to decide their majors for college. In the end, based on this graph students may choose one of these careers solely on money.  However, I wonder if this information is completely accurate for students in fours years who may have to decide their fields of study now. Not only that but there are many other factors that contribute to deciding one's field of study. Therefore, I don't think this graph is beneficial as one piece of evidence for jobs or career paths solely based on over generalized wages which in the end may end up changing overtime.

comments.raw_comment: Douglas Webber in his “The Lifetime Earnings Premia of Different Majors” analyzes projected career income from solely an economical standpoint. Looking at the graph, I noticed that the bottom half of the careers focus mostly on the STEM subjects. The careers that earn a lesser amount money appear to be geared more towards social-oriented subjects, such as philosophy and education. The white dashes on the bars are the median earnings, and the darker shades of blue are the points nearest to the median. It is questionable if this graph is really proportional, as well as if the graph is accurate. I am unaware of where the author received his information, causing me to feel quite skeptical of the graph. I am curious as to how many incomes were utilized in order to create this bar graph and if taxes were included or removed from the overall earnings. This graph could be indicating how as a society, we have drifted away from more social careers in favor of technology.

comments.raw_comment: The general trend of the graph seems to reflect that STEM-based career paths tend to result in higher projected career earnings than language-based or social science-based careers. This trend implies that people do not value the language and social-based careers enough even though I believe they do play a significant role in the infrastructure of society and the development of citizens’ minds. Also, while the median career earning does increase from the top to bottom of the graph, the range between the 10th and 90th percentiles also generally increases. The greater dispersion of career earnings may be a result of many people wanting to go into higher paying careers. Greater competition would be generated, causing a wider spectrum in the amount of money people in the same career path can earn. Thus, job availability should be taken into consideration along with the projected earnings. It is not wise to choose a career path based solely on the information shown by this graph because it is lacking the consideration of factors without a monetary incentive, such as satisfaction and passion—it is important for people to love their careers. I wonder how the data on this graph was collected and whether it only reflects the projected earnings for only a certain group of college graduates in society or whether it reflects all college graduates. I am curious to know if factors such as the university someone attends or their race/ethnicity can alter what the graph currently displays.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that as the careers become more related to fields in STEM, the median earnings increase. While I agree to some extent that the graph portrays a realistic visual of average career earnings, I believe that it has failed to take into account other factors beside the field of the career. Jobs like computer science and chemical engineer are becoming more popular amongst college students, which might make the supply for these jobs less demanding. With more people applying for similar positions, companies can pay workers lower salaries. Another factor, besides supply and demand, is passion. What the graph fails to consider is that some college students choose a certain career path out of passion or love for a subject. By categorizing the careers based on their earnings, Webber is associating careers with the amount of money that is earned. I agree that money should factor into considering a career, but it should not be the sole factor in determining a certain path.

comments.raw_comment: As indicated by the graph, the median wage for different careers fields increases as the graph progresses from top to bottom. In addition, most of the careers with median wages of $3 million or higher are STEM based, while careers with median wages that fall below $3M are based primarily on sociology, language, history, or the arts. I wonder if such discrepancy between career types is due to a higher demand for workers in scientific and mathematical fields, than others that fall outside of STEM. Although there are exceptions to this rule, the general pattern of the graph supports the idea that the economy favors STEM based careers. In my opinion, the graph seems to advise college students deciding on a major to enter these fields, using solely money as a motivation. I personally disagree with the notion that one should reconsider their major based on earnings alone because these statistics are subject to change and if one has no business in chemical engineering, then they should not enter such a career they are not adept at, nor take interest, in for the pay. Though I concede that sufficient salary is important as well as job availability, they should not be the only criteria in deciding a major, and thus the graph should be used as a supplement in a decision, not the sole deciding factor.

comments.raw_comment: As I was observing these graphs I noticed that between the 10th and 25th percentile, even a chemical engineer can make as much as the average person studying psychology. I believe the reason for this falls under supply and demand. Even though Chemical Engineering can be considered as a much more difficult job than Psychology, it all depends on if the place where they live really needs a Psychologist or a Chemical Engineer. So for this reason, when looking at the 75th to 90th percentile I see that the Chemical Engineer can make 5 or 6 times more than a Psychologist not because it might be a more difficult job, but because there is a plethora of psychologists, and a scarce amount of Chemical Engineers. With the idea of supply and demand comes the fact that companies or businesses rely more on efficiency to meet the demand. This means that all workers have an expiration date and when they reach the peak of their productivity, they could easily be replaced by others willing to work harder and more efficiently.

Douglas Webber analyzes the benefits of different careers from an economic standpoint, demonstrating which career college graduates can ultimately gain the most wealth from. Webber contends that money should be the greatest influence in one’s career choice through his indirect support of students choosing careers which will give them the greatest wealth over factors such as passion or interest. His graph may also give inaccurate results as he is simply speculating over the amount of money people could make in their lifetime in a career, as demand could rise or fall, leading to an increase of decrease in income made. He also demonstrates a bias by his favoring of mainly STEM majors as careers with the highest earnings. Surely, there are many other careers which earn large sums of money and are not STEM, and by not including these majors, he attempts to persuade the observer to choose STEM careers in order earn the most wealth.

comments.raw_comment: The graph displayed depicts the career earnings for college graduates in specific areas of study. Firstly, the graph has two colors, light blue and dark blue, the dark blue representing the average earnings, and the light blue to represent the outliers, or the highest and lowest, in the pay scale. Another observation is that the careers that live in the areas of math and science tend to make more money over time than the careers based in the areas of literature, art, and critical thinking. This graph, while giving a good prediction of the earning, is flawed. It does not take into account the different factors that affect the earnings in some careers such as: level of education, working environment, passion for that field, inflation over time, the effect of government control over some careers like education, or criminal justice, and it does not take into account the different jobs that can be obtained with these different careers. While this graph gives a general overview of the earnings that can be obtained when following certain areas of study, it is not a good reference to choose a future career.

comments.raw_comment: The graph represents the projected career earnings for college graduates based on their major. Although, the graph appears to be a credible source, the sheer fact that the data is a “projection” implies that it could be incredibly inaccurate. The demand and funding for specific career options is constantly fluctuating and especially in the event of a severe economic crisis, specific earnings could plummet or skyrocket unexpectedly. Additionally, the graph can be misleading in the fact that the lowest and highest 10 percent of the projected career earnings are left off the chart. Therefore, if someone enters in the field expecting to make a certain amount, they may be unhappily surprised to realize they are in the lowest percentile and earning severely less than expected. Furthermore, low projections may discourage students from majoring in a field that may be best suited for them, and lose the opportunity to thrive at a job they excel at. I wonder what the reach of this graph is, and whether or not it will impact the decision of college students.

comments.raw_comment: The graph contends that higher paying jobs are typically associated with STEM majors. It utilizes a comparison between the medians of projected career earnings in different fields. However, the graph is not omniscient. It attempts to predict wages years into the future, which can be highly inaccurate. For example, the economics field is set as the second greatest money earner, yet if there were a horrific stock market collapse tomorrow, the economics would quickly fall down the ranks of top paying jobs. The graph is intended as a guide for students deciding on their major, yet it leaves itself vulnerable to unforeseen changes years in the future. Students should not use the graph as their sole source of advice when it comes to career choice, especially since they will leave college jobless and in desperate need of a way to pay off their debt. However, the graph does aid in revealing the current state of careers since it is based on recently updated information. It also has a more expansive amount of data available to viewers to inform them of the current job climate. It does have its uses, but it should not be viewed as the law of the land.

For example, career choices of education, social work, or philosophy are projected to earn much less than careers such as chemical, or electrical engineering. This illustrates a very prevalent issue. We don’t want to be examined or have our communities changed but rather we support industries that serve to enhance our day to day lives. New technology products help individuals better their lives whereas careers that produce thought and incite understanding have much less appeal to our increasingly materialistic world. Non-STEM careers remain relatively unattractive to the current society because we don’t want to necessarily take the time or energy to think about our society.

comments.raw_comment:
One of my first observations was that the professions are ordered by median in increasing order. I also observe that there is considerable variation within each profession and think that perhaps there is less (though still significant) variation between the professions. As a college student studying math and humanities, I found it comforting to observe that there is a lot of overlap - it might be less likely, but a philosophy major sometimes earns more than an economics major. 

I notice that nursing is far down (higher lifetime earnings) and that surprises me. I'd like to know more about who was counted as a nursing major and whether those students trained solely to be nurses or whether perhaps some were pre-med and went on to be doctors.

That brings me to my biggest point: thinking in terms of majors can be deceptive. English majors can become chemistry PhDs. Psychology majors can join PR firms. I've read that kids from wealthier backgrounds often have more freedom to do "riskier" humanities majors - some of them then end up in law or finance. Overall, I think this graph might be trying to tell a story about how choice of major can affect lifetime earnings, but I think there is a lot not said that my fellow students should consider. We need to remember that major does not dictate career path, and thus the graph does not necessarily reflect how much people actually working in the areas they majored in earn.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice in the graph that there is a pretty significant pay gap between most careers and the chemical engineering careers. One thing I wondered was why people majoring in important things such as education earn less than business majors. Based on the graph, I can infer that the reason for why people in majors such as education, criminal justice, and social work, which altogether seem like very important parts of a society, are earning less is because modern technology and culture is taking away the traditional importance of these things in society.
I think that the deeper story that the graph is telling is that there should be some reconsideration for federal wages in professions that are extremely valuable to society such as education and criminal justice. People who work in criminal justice and education are the framers of society and should be deemed as more important. They often do hard work and have to deal with things that many people prefer not to deal with. For this reason, they should also be considered equally as important as the people earning higher wages than them.

Chemical engineering, which according to the graph seems he most enticing, has a much slower growth than say computer science and thus is not nearly as secure. In addition, work hours st be considered. The biggest reason education earns the least is due to the fact that it is a government job. Yet, government jobs have far lower hours compared to private sector jobs and may thus be more enticing than it seems when glancing at this graph. America’s youth must realize that the nuances of careers are increasingly important as competition is rising in the new global economy. The future is daunting, but America’s youth can surely prepare.

Thanks to all teachers and students who responded to our graph on the earning power of college graduates by major.  How much you make in a career isn’t the only criteria for selecting a major, but did this graph change your thinking about your college major and future career?

Lots of questions came up from this graph.  You asked how the majors were selected, how projected earnings were calculated, and how many years is considered a lifetime.  You wondered about what the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentile means and why the blue segments are of different lengths.  But, most frequently, you noticed that education majors made less than STEM majors.  As O'BryantGirlNamedFallon from Boston wrote, “Well, to me it seems like the teachers, who shape the future of our children, are not getting the money they deserve. I wonder, why should the teachers who help all these people reach their dreams, why should they get the lowest pay?” 

Since we continue to post responses, is there more that you notice?  More that you wonder?  Talk to your classmates and read the moderators’ responses. Maybe something they say will lead to more things you notice, wonder, and conjecture. 

Check back on Thursday, January 11 to learn more about this graph. We hope to see you again next month on Tuesday, February 13 for our next "What's Going On In This Graph?"   Signing off now -- Sharon in Boston and Erica in Pittsburgh. See you in February for our special Valentine’s Day graph!

comments.raw_comment: I notice that wages seem to be skewed in favor of more technical-oriented professions, such as computer science, medicine, or mathematics, which is interesting since it implies that the more societal-oriented--such as education, humanities, history--are no longer as important. A chemical engineer, from the looks of this graph, would be much better off than a chemistry teacher, even though a teacher would help to serve society through educating the next generations. This makes me wonder, then, how many people actually achieve this profession. How many graduated with a high degree, and how many graduated from a prestigious university? If there are many educators living off a lower pay, and yet a few computer engineers making twice their lifetime earnings, it could be a danger to the distribution of wealth, the welfare of the classes, and the future of the next generations. The story this graph is telling could be that as a society, we have drifted closer to technology than ever before--maybe more than we are to each other, and the well-being of the many.
